claim: Manual gestures and speech recruit a common neural network, involving Broca's area in the left hemisphere.
source: Manual gestures and speech recruit a common neural network, involving Broca's area in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data from this study.

claim: Speech-gesture integration gave rise to theories on the critical role of manual gesturing in the origin of language.
source: Such speech-gesture integration gave rise to theories on the critical role of manual gesturing in the origin of language.
evidence: This refers to existing theoretical frameworks in the literature.

claim: Both direction and degree of gestural communication's handedness are associated and correlated with contralateral depth asymmetry at the ventral portion of the Inferior Arcuate sulcus in baboons.
source: In fact, both direction and degree of gestural communication's handedness – but not handedness for object manipulation are associated and correlated with contralateral depth asymmetry at this exact IA sulcus portion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on MRI measurements and behavioral data from 50 baboons.

claim: Baboons that prefer to communicate with their right hand have a deeper left-than-right IA sulcus than those preferring to communicate with their left hand.
source: In other words, baboons that prefer to communicate with their right hand have a deeper left-than-right IA sulcus, than those preferring to communicate with their left hand and vice versa.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the study's data findings.

claim: Gestural communication's lateralisation is not associated with the Central sulcus depth asymmetry.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to handedness for object manipulation, gestural communication's lateralisation is not associated to the Central sulcus depth asymmetry, suggesting a double dissociation of handedness' types between manipulative action and gestural communication.
evidence: This is based on the study's findings comparing different sulci and handedness types.

claim: There is a double dissociation of handedness types between manipulative action and gestural communication.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to handedness for object manipulation, gestural communication's lateralisation is not associated to the Central sulcus depth asymmetry, suggesting a double dissociation of handedness' types between manipulative action and gestural communication.
evidence: This is inferred from the contrasting patterns of association between different handedness types and brain regions.

claim: The specific gestural lateralisation signature within the baboons' frontal cortex might reflect a phylogenetical continuity with language-related Broca lateralisation in humans.
source: It is thus not excluded that this specific gestural lateralisation signature within the baboons' frontal cortex might reflect a phylogenetical continuity with language-related Broca lateralisation in humans.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in an evolutionary context.

claim: Broca's area has historically been considered as the centre of speech production.
source: Broca's area and its left hemispheric specialisation has historically been considered as the centre of speech production.
evidence: This refers to historical scientific understanding.

claim: Broca's area remains a key node for language specialisation within a neural distributed network.
source: Even if such a modular conception of language's neural bases was questioned by models of plastic and large distributed networks (Friederici, 2017; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007), it is still well acknowledged that Broca's area remains a key node for language specialisation within this neural distributed network.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Broca's area functions as an interface between speech and multimodal motor integration including gesture and mouth movements.
source: Complementary work thereby highlighted Broca's area as an interface between speech and multimodal motor integration including gesture and mouth mouvements (Gentilucci and Dalla Volta, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Broca's area is involved in motor planning, sequential, and hierarchical organization of behaviours, such as linguistic grammar or tool use and tool making.
source: Broca's area is also known for its involvement in motor planning, sequential, and hierarchical organization of behaviours, such as linguistic grammar or tool use and tool making (Gentilucci and Dalla Volta, 2008; Koechlin and Jubault, 2006; Stout et al., 2015; Corballis, 2015; Wakita, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Language organisation took some of its phylogenetical roots into a gestural system across primate evolution.
source: Therefore, a growing number of researchers proposed that language organisation took some of its phylogenetical roots into a gestural system across primate evolution (Gentilucci and Dalla Volta, 2008; Corballis, 2015; Tomasello, 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Nonhuman primate studies have documented continuities of the communicative gestural system with key features of human language such as intentionality, referentiality, learning flexibility, and lateralisation.
source: A large body of nonhuman primate studies has documented some continuities of the communicative gestural system with several key features of human language such as intentionality, referentiality, learning flexibility, and lateralisation (e.g. Tomasello, 2008; Meguerditchian and Vauclair, 2014; Molesti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Studies in baboons and great apes have shown that communicative manual gesturing elicited stronger right-hand use in comparison to non-communicative manipulative actions at a populational-level.
source: About manual lateralisation specifically, studies in baboons and great apes have indeed shown that communicative manual gesturing elicited stronger right-hand use in comparison to non-communicative manipulative actions at a populational-level (reviewed in: Meguerditchian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: A double dissociation concerning the type of handedness has been documented between gestural communication and object manipulation in primates.
source: In addition, at the individual level, a double dissociation concerning the type of handedness has been documented between gestural communication and object manipulation, showing that primates classified as right-handed for communicative gesture are not especially classified as right-handed for object manipulation and vice versa (Meguerditchian and Vauclair, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most left-handers (78%) show left-hemisphere dominance for language.
source: This is consistent with human literature showing that typical object-manipulation handedness measures turned out to be a rather poor marker of language lateralisation (Fagard, 2013), as most left-handers (78%) also show left-hemisphere dominance for language (Knecht et al., 2000; Mazoyer et al., 2014), just like right-handed people.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: Direction of handedness for object manipulation was found associated to contralateral asymmetries of the motor hand area within the Central sulcus in both humans and nonhuman primates.
source: In both humans and nonhuman primates, direction of handedness for object manipulation was found associated to contralateral asymmetries of the motor hand area within the Central sulcus (e.g. humans: Amunts et al., 2000; Cykowski et al., 2008; chimpanzees: Hopkins and Cantalupo, 2004; Dadda et al., 2006; Baboons: Margiotoudi et al., 2019; Capuchin monkeys: Phillips and Sherwood, 2005; Squirrel monkeys: Nudo et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations across species.

claim: The neural substrates of typical handedness measures and language brain organisation might be independent from each other.
source: In fact, it has recently been demonstrated that the neural substrates of typical handedness measures and language brain organisation might be not related but rather independent from each other (Groen et al., 2013; Ocklenburg et al., 2014; Häberling et al., 2016; Labache et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: The degree of right-handedness for preverbal gestures is more pronounced at a populational-level than handedness for manipulation in early human development.
source: In early human development, the degree of right-handedness for preverbal gestures is more pronounced at a populational-level than handedness for manipulation (Blake et al., 1994; Bonvillian et al., 1997; see also Fagard, 2013; Cochet and Vauclair, 2010) and increases when the lexical spurt occurs in children contrary to manipulation handedness (Cochet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: Broca's area is activated in the left hemisphere for sign language production including manual and oro-facial gestures.
source: Moreover, further work showed Broca's activation in the left hemisphere also for sign language production including manual and oro-facial gestures (Emmorey et al., 2004; MacSweeney et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroimaging studies.

claim: Nonhuman primates have shown gross left-hemispheric asymmetries of homologous language areas at a populational level that are similar to those described in humans.
source: This hypothesis might be relevant to investigate given brain studies in nonhuman primates have shown gross left-hemispheric asymmetries of homologous language areas at a populational level that are similar to the ones described in humans (e.g., Geschwind and Levitsky, 1968; Keller et al., 2009): In particular Broca's homologue in great apes (Cantalupo and Hopkins, 2001; Graïc et al., 2020) as well as the Planum Temporale in great apes and even in baboons, an Old World monkey species, in both adult and newborns (Gannon et al., 1998; Marie et al., 2018; Becker et al., 2021a; Becker et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to comparative neuroanatomical studies.

claim: No study regarding structural asymmetry for Broca's homologue has been investigated in Old World monkeys.
source: For Old World monkeys specifically, no study regarding structural asymmetry for Broca's homologue has been investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of previous research.

claim: The inferior precentral sulcus, the inferior frontal sulcus and the fronto-orbital sulcus are absent in monkeys.
source: In fact, the inferior precentral sulcus, the inferior frontal sulcus and the fronto-orbital sulcus, which are common borders of Broca's homologue in apes (Cantalupo and Hopkins, 2001), are absent in monkeys and thus delimitation is not trivial.
evidence: This is based on comparative neuroanatomical knowledge with citation.

claim: The mid-ventral and ventral portion of the Inferior Arcuate sulcus is the epicentre of Broca's homologue in Old World monkeys.
source: Nevertheless, all the detailed cytoarchitectonic studies addressing the Broca's homologue within the frontal lobe in Old World monkeys (i.e. in mostly macaques but also in baboons) – and its two components Area 44 and 45 – pointed towards the same sulcus of interest as the epicentre of this region: the mid-ventral and ventral portion of the Inferior Arcuate sulcus (IA sulcus).
evidence: This is based on synthesis of cytoarchitectonic studies.

claim: The IA sulcus is considered homologue to the ascending branch of the inferior precentral sulcus.
source: The IA sulcus is considered homologue to the ascending branch of the inferior precentral sulcus (Amiez and Petrides, 2009) which delimits Broca's area posteriorly in humans and great apes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to comparative neuroanatomy.

claim: Area 45 homologue sits in the anterior bank of the ventral IA sulcus in monkeys.
source: In monkeys, Area 45 homologue sits in the anterior bank of the ventral IA sulcus (Petrides et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to cytoarchitectonic research.

claim: Area 44 homologue might be located in the fundus and the posterior bank of the ventral IA sulcus in monkeys.
source: In contrast, Area 44 homologue might be located in the fundus and the posterior bank of the ventral IA sulcus in monkeys (Petrides et al., 2005), which overlaps with F5 region related to the mirror neuron system (Belmalih et al., 2009; Rizzolatti and Fogassi, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cytoarchitectonic and functional studies.

claim: Electric stimulation in the fundus of the ventral IA sulcus elicited oro-facial and finger movements in macaques.
source: Electric stimulation in the fundus of the ventral IA sulcus elicited oro-facial and finger mouvements in macaques (Petrides et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental stimulation studies.

claim: A cytoarchitectonic study showed Area 45 anteriorly to the IA sulcus in baboons.
source: Concerning baboons specifically, a cytoarchitectonic study (Watanabe-Sawaguchi et al., 1991) showed similarities to the macaque frontal lobe organisation given Area 45 anteriorly to the IA sulcus, even if Area 44 was not described (Petrides et al., 2005; Belmalih et al., 2009; Rizzolatti and Fogassi, 2014; Watanabe-Sawaguchi et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cytoarchitectonic studies.

claim: The depth of the ventral part of the IA sulcus constitutes the only critical neuroanatomical marker for delimiting the border and the surface of Broca's homologue in monkeys.
source: Therefore, in the absence of the usual Broca's sulcal borders found in apes, the depth of the ventral part of the IA sulcus constitutes the only critical neuroanatomical marker for delimiting the border and the surface of Broca's homologue in monkeys.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative neuroanatomical discussion.

claim: Between baboons communicating preferentially with the right hand versus the ones with the left hand, there are significant contralateral differences of depth asymmetries in the ventral portion of the IA sulcus from positions 65-95.
source: Between baboons communicating preferentially with the right hand versus the ones with the left hand, we found significant contralateral differences of depth asymmetries in the ventral portion of the IA sulcus (i.e., from the mid-ventral IA position to the most ventral IA sulcus portion, namely from contiguous positions 65–95 out of the 99 segmented positions of the entire IA sulcus) according to a cluster-based permutation test (p < .01, t-value clustermass = 76.16, for p < .01 a clustermass of 65.28 was needed, see Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on statistical analysis of MRI data.

claim: The 28 baboons using preferentially their right hand for communicative gestures showed more leftward IA sulcus depth asymmetry at the ventral cluster than the 22 ones using preferentially their left-hand.
source: In other words, the 28 baboons using preferentially their right hand for communicative gestures showed more leftward IA sulcus depth asymmetry at this cluster than the 22 ones using preferentially their left-hand.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the statistical findings.

claim: For non-communicative manipulative actions, there was no significant difference of sulcus depth asymmetries between the left- versus right-handed groups concerning any portion of the IA sulcus.
source: In contrast, for non-communicative manipulative actions, we found no significant difference of sulcus depth asymmetries between the left- (N = 22) versus right-handed (N = 28) groups concerning any portion of the IA sulcus, according to a cluster-based permutation test (p > .10) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between individual AQ depth values of the Broca's cluster (positions 65-95) and individual handedness degree for communication.
source: In addition, after calculating the AQ score per subject representing the sulcus depth asymmetry of the whole 'Broca's cluster' (i.e. from the sum of the IA sulcus depths from positions 65–95 in the left hemisphere and the sum of IA sulcus depths from position 65–95 in the right hemisphere), we found a significant negative correlation between individual AQ depth values of the Broca's cluster (i.e. from positions 65–95) and individual handedness degree for communication (HI): r(48) = –.337; p < .05 (i.e. The stronger the hand preference is for one hand, the deeper is the IA sulcus asymmetry from positions 65 to 95 in the contralateral hemisphere) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: AQ depth values of the Broca's cluster did not show significant correlation with HI for non-communicative actions.
source: In contrast, AQ depth values of the Broca's cluster did not show significant correlation with HI for non-communicative actions (r(48) = –.037; p ≈ 1) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a significant difference between the correlation of Broca's cluster AQ with communication handedness versus the correlation with action handedness.
source: Using the cocor package in R (Diedenhofen and Musch, 2015), a comparison between these two overlapping correlations based on dependent groups showed a significant difference between the two correlations (p < .05).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of correlations.

claim: There was no significant difference of sulcus depth asymmetries in the Central sulcus regarding communicative gestures.
source: When comparing with the control sulcus of interest, the Central sulcus related to the primary motor cortex, an opposite effect was found between handedness for manipulative actions and hand preferences for communicative gesture. We found no significant difference of sulcus depth asymmetries regarding communicative gestures.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis.

claim: The Central sulcus presented a contralateral asymmetry at continuous positions 56-60 for non-communicative manipulative actions.
source: In contrast, Margiotoudi et al., 2019 reported that the CS presented a contralateral asymmetry at continuous positions 56–60 (labelled as the 'Motor-hand area's cluster') for non-communicative manipulative actions, after permutation tests for correction (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on citation to a previous study by the same research group.

claim: There was a significant main effect on the AQ scores for communication handedness (F1,46 = 14.08, p < .01).
source: The mixed-model analysis of variance demonstrated a significant main effect on the AQ scores for communication handedness (F1,46 = 14.08, p < .01) and for action handedness (F1,46 = 4,1, p < .05).
evidence: This is a primary finding from statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect on the AQ scores for action handedness (F1,46 = 4.1, p < .05).
source: The mixed-model analysis of variance demonstrated a significant main effect on the AQ scores for communication handedness (F1,46 = 14.08, p < .01) and for action handedness (F1,46 = 4,1, p < .05).
evidence: This is a primary finding from statistical analysis.

claim: The IA sulcus left- or rightward depth asymmetry at its mid-ventral and ventral portion is associated exclusively with contralateral direction of communicative manual gestures' lateralisation in baboons but not handedness for non-communicative actions.
source: We showed that the IA sulcus left- or rightward depth asymmetry at its mid-ventral and ventral portion (labelled as the 'Broca cluster') is associated exclusively with contralateral direction (left-/right-hand) of communicative manual gestures' lateralisation in baboons but not handedness for non-communicative actions.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Individuals with a stronger degree of manual lateralisation for communicative gesture have greater IA sulcus depth asymmetries at the ventral cluster in the hemisphere contralateral to their preferred hand for communication.
source: In other words, individuals with a stronger degree of manual lateralisation for communicative gesture have greater IA sulcus depth asymmetries at this ventral cluster in the hemisphere contralateral to their preferred hand for communication.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation findings.

claim: The ventral positions of sulcal depth asymmetries are at a crossroad of Broca-related frontal regions including the fundus of the sulcus, Area 44, the anterior bank Area 45, the posterior bank and ventral F5 or granual frontal area.
source: The ventral positions of such sulcal depth asymmetries are clearly at a crossroad of Broca-related frontal regions including the fundus of the sulcus, Area 44 (Petrides et al., 2005), the anterior bank, Area 45 (Petrides et al., 2005), the posterior bank and ventral F5 or granual frontal area (GrF) (Belmalih et al., 2009; Rizzolatti and Fogassi, 2014).
evidence: This is based on integration of the findings with cited neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The sulcus' depth might reflect a gyral surface and its underlying grey matter volume.
source: Since the sulcus' depth might reflect a gyral surface and its underlying grey matter volume, future work of delineating and quantifying grey matter of the ventral IA sulcus would help determining which of those sub-regions of the Broca homologue is driving the asymmetry specifically, for instance by VBM methods.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the interpretation of sulcal depth measures.

claim: Handedness for manipulative actions in baboons was previously found related to the motor cortex asymmetry within the Central sulcus.
source: Whereas handedness for manipulative actions in baboons was previously found related to the motor cortex asymmetry within the Central sulcus (Margiotoudi et al., 2019), our present findings report the first evidence in monkeys that the neurostructural lateralisation's landmark of communicative gesture is located in a frontal region, related to Broca's homologue.
evidence: This is based on citation to a previous study.

claim: The present findings report the first evidence in monkeys that the neurostructural lateralisation's landmark of communicative gesture is located in a frontal region, related to Broca's homologue.
source: Whereas handedness for manipulative actions in baboons was previously found related to the motor cortex asymmetry within the Central sulcus (Margiotoudi et al., 2019), our present findings report the first evidence in monkeys that the neurostructural lateralisation's landmark of communicative gesture is located in a frontal region, related to Broca's homologue.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: The contrast of results between manipulation and communication found at the cortical level is consistent with what was found at the behavioural level in studies showing that communicative gesture in baboons and chimpanzees elicited specific and independent patterns of manual lateralisation in comparison to non-communicative manipulative actions.
source: Such a contrast of results between manipulation and communication found at the cortical level is consistent with what was found at the behavioural level in studies showing that communicative gesture in baboons and chimpanzees elicited specific and independent patterns of manual lateralisation in comparison to non-communicative manipulative actions (Meguerditchian and Vauclair, 2009; Meguerditchian et al., 2010).
evidence: This integrates the current findings with cited behavioral studies.

claim: Gestural communication's lateralisation in nonhuman primates might be related to a different lateralised neural system than handedness for pure manipulative action.
source: Therefore, it provides additional support to the hypothesis suggesting that gestural communication's lateralisation in nonhuman primates might be, just as language brain organisation in human (see Häberling et al., 2016), related to a different lateralised neural system than handedness for pure manipulative action.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings with reference to human literature.

claim: The specific correlates with Broca's homologue's lateralisation is consistent with what was found in chimpanzees.
source: Its specific correlates with Broca's homologue's lateralisation is also consistent with what was found in our closest relatives, the chimpanzee (Taglialatela et al., 2006; Meguerditchian et al., 2012).
evidence: This compares the findings to cited studies in chimpanzees.

claim: A functional segregation was proposed with Broca's anterior part implicated in language syntax and its posterior part exclusively implicated in motor actions.
source: Regarding Broca's area in humans, very recently, a functional segregation was proposed with Broca's anterior part implicated in language syntax and its posterior part exclusively implicated in motor actions (Zaccarella et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on a citation to recent human neuroscience research.

claim: The intentionality of primate's communicative gesture might account for the hypothesised functional interface of actions and language prerequisites, nested inside the monkeys' Broca's homologue.
source: In an evolutionary perspective we propose therefore that the intentionality of primate's communicative gesture might account for this hypothesised functional interface of actions and language prerequisites, nested inside the monkeys' Broca's homologue (see also: Rizzolatti and Craighero, 2004Arbib et al., 2008; Rizzolatti and Fogassi, 2014; Corballis, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: In macaques Broca's homologue, neuronal recordings showed populations of specific neurons activated for both volitional vocal and manual actions.
source: In addition, in macaques Broca's homologue, neuronal recordings showed populations of specific neurons activated for both volitional vocal and manual actions (Gavrilov and Nieder, 2021).
evidence: This is based on a citation to neurophysiological research.

claim: Gestural communication may be a compelling modality for one of the multimodal evolutionary roots of the typical multimodal language system in humans and its hemispheric specialisation.
source: The articulation of our results with this recent literature suggests that gestural communication may be a compelling modality for one of the multimodal evolutionary roots of the typical multimodal language system in humans and its hemispheric specialisation.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation of the findings.

claim: Language-related frontal lateralisation might be inherited from a gestural communicative system dating back to the common ancestor of humans, great apes and Old World monkeys, 25-35 million years ago.
source: It is thus not excluded that language-related frontal lateralisation might be much older than previously thought and inherited from a gestural communicative system dating back, not to Hominid origins, but rather to the common ancestor of humans, great apes and Old World monkeys, 25–35 million years ago.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Inter-hemispheric asymmetries of the IA sulcus' depth were quantified from anatomical T1w MRI images in 80 baboons Papio anubis.
source: Inter-hemispheric asymmetries of the IA sulcus' depth were quantified from anatomical T1w MRI images in 80 baboons Papio anubis born in captivity and free from developmental or anatomical abnormalities or brain disorders (generation F1, 52 females, 28 males, age range = 7–32 years, mean age (years): M = 17.7, SE = 5.9).
evidence: This describes the methods and sample of the study.

claim: The final sample included 50 baboons who combined both types of measures of handedness and the depth measures of the two sulci of interest in the two hemispheres of the brain.
source: It resulted a total overlap of 50 baboons (29 females and 21 males, mean age (years): M = 12.3, SE = 5.8) who combined thus the both types of measures of handedness (communication versus manipulation) and the depth measures of the two sulci of interest (IA sulcus and Central sulcus) in the two hemispheres of the brain.
evidence: This describes the final sample used in the analysis.

claim: The IA sulcus and the Central sulcus were extracted from T1w images using the pipeline of the free BrainVisa software.
source: The IA sulcus and the Central sulcus were extracted from T1w images using the pipeline of the free BrainVisa software (see Mangin et al., 2004 for details of the procedure).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach.

claim: The sulcus parametrization tool within the BrainVisa toolbox subdivides the sulci of each hemisphere into 99 standardized positions from dorsal to ventral sulcus extremities.
source: The sulcus parametrization tool within the BrainVisa toolbox provides therefore sulcus-based morphometry by subdividing the sulci of each hemisphere into 99 standardized positions from dorsal to ventral sulcus extremities in order to quantify the variation of sulcal depth all across the sulci's 99 positions (Mangin et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach with citation.

claim: The hand slapping behaviour is the most common and frequent visual gesture of the baboon repertoire.
source: Indeed, the hand slapping behaviour – a probably innate gestures used by the baboon to threat or intimidate the recipient – is the most common and frequent visual gesture of the repertoire (Molesti et al., 2020) produced intentionally and unimanually in a lateralised manner across similar agonistic contexts and similar emitter's postures (Meguerditchian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Among the 50 baboons, 22 subjects were classified as left-handed and 28 as right-handed for communicative gesture.
source: Among the 50 baboons, for communicative gesture, 22 subjects were thus classified as left-handed, 28 as right-handed following the HI direction.
evidence: This describes the distribution of handedness in the sample.

claim: For object-related manipulative actions, 22 subjects were classified as left-handed and 28 as right-handed.
source: For object-related manipulative actions (i.e. the bimanual tube task), 22 subjects were classified as left-handed, 28 as right-handed as already reported in Margiotoudi et al., 2019 for those 50 overlapping subjects.
evidence: This describes the distribution of handedness in the sample with citation.

claim: Among the 50 baboons, 18 subjects switched left-/right-handed categories of hand preference between communicative gesture and manipulative actions.
source: Among the 50 baboons, 18 subjects switched left-/right-handed categories of hand preference between communicative gesture and manipulative actions (i.e. 9 from left-handed group for gestural communication to right-handed group for manipulative actions, 9 from right-handed group for gestural communication to left-handed group for manipulative actions).
evidence: This describes the behavioral data showing dissociation between handedness types.

claim: Statistical analysis was conducted using R 3.6.1 by Cluster Mass Permutation tests.
source: Statistical analysis was conducted using R 3.6.1 by Cluster Mass Permutation tests (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).
evidence: This describes the statistical methods used.

claim: Figure 1 shows significant contralateral AQ difference (p < .01) between right-handed and left-handed groups for communicative gesture at IA sulcus positions 65 to 95.
source: Significant contralateral AQ difference (p < .01) between the two groups was found for a cluster including positions 65 to 95 (highlighted in purple in the graph and the 3D representation of the IA Sulcus).
evidence: This refers to data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Figure 2A shows a significant negative correlation between HI for communicative gestures and AQ depth values of the Broca's cluster.
source: (A) Individual handedness degree (HI) for communicative gestures and AQ depth values of the Broca's cluster (i.e. from positions 65–95) in dark blue dots. Light blue line: Significant negative correlation between HI and AQ.
evidence: This refers to data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Figure 2B shows a non-significant correlation between HI for non-communicative manipulative actions and AQ depth values of the Broca's cluster.
source: B. Individual handedness degree (HI) for non-communicative manipulative actions (HI) and AQ depth values of the Broca's cluster (i.e. from positions 65–95) in dark green squares. Light green line (superposing on x axis): Non-significant correlation between HI and AQ.
evidence: This refers to data shown in Figure 2B.
